sentences.text: Monday at Contoso.
An employee writes to Nexo, the I T agent: my laptop will not turn on, and I want to know how my other case is going.
One message, two wishes.
Nexo has a topic that creates tickets, and another that checks ticket status.
Something has to decide what to do with this message.
That decision is called orchestration.
By the end of this class you will know the two ways to make it, and the three harnesses behind them.
Here is the picture to keep.
Orchestration is a receptionist.
The classic receptionist has a list of phrases.
A visitor says something, and the receptionist sends them to the one department whose phrases match best.
The generative receptionist understands what the person wants, and can send them to several departments, one after another.
Same building, very different service.
In standard harness agents there are two modes.
With classic orchestration, the agent triggers the topic whose trigger phrases are most similar to what the user typed.
A trigger phrase is an example sentence you write on the topic, like check my ticket or where is my case.
Nexo's message matches one topic better than the other, so only one topic runs.
The second wish is simply lost.
With generative orchestration, the agent uses A I to decide which topic, tool, other agent or knowledge source to use.
New agents use generative orchestration by default.
If you create the agent from a prebuilt one, its configuration decides which mode is used.
So unless something says otherwise, your new agent starts with the generative receptionist.
What changes in practice?
Topics: generative picks them by description, classic by trigger phrases.
Tools: generative calls them by name and description, classic only calls them explicitly from a topic.
Knowledge: generative can search it proactively, classic uses it as a fallback when no topic matches.
Several items: generative combines them in one answer.
Missing data: generative asks for it on its own.
And generative writes the response itself.
Your turn.
An agent uses classic orchestration.
A maker adds a tool with a perfect name and description, and expects the agent to choose it on its own when users ask.
Will it work?
Yes, because the description is very clear?
No, classic only calls tools from a topic?
Or yes, but only as a fallback choice here?
Decide before I answer.
No.
In classic orchestration tools are only called from a topic.
Choosing them is a generative skill.
In generative mode, the most important factor for choosing is the description of each topic, tool, agent or knowledge source.
The name and the input and output parameters also matter.
A good description is short, one or two sentences, in active voice.
It includes keywords the user would say.
And it also says what it does not do.
That last part draws the border between neighbours.
Here is what goes wrong.
If two descriptions are similar, the agent picks only one, and the result is unpredictable.
So Contoso writes clearly different ones.
Ticket status: checks the status of an existing ticket, does not create tickets.
Create ticket: creates a new ticket, does not check existing ones.
And when you turn on generative mode in an older agent, Copilot Studio generates descriptions from the trigger phrases.
Review them.
Your turn.
A generative agent has two topics, reset password and unlock account.
Sometimes one runs, sometimes the other, for the same request.
What should the maker fix?
Switch the agent to classic orchestration instead?
Add many more trigger phrases to both topics?
Or rewrite both descriptions so they differ?
Decide before I answer.
Rewrite the descriptions.
In generative mode, overlapping descriptions make selection unpredictable.
Now watch Nexo in generative mode.
It detects two intentions.
It calls Ticket status with the case number it took from the conversation.
Then it calls Create ticket, and asks only for the data that is still missing.
Finally it writes a single response that covers both wishes.
A topic can even return its result as an output variable instead of a message, so the agent combines it with everything else.

scenes.title: Turn it on, watch it work

sentences.text: Where is the switch?
In Settings, in the generative A I section, under orchestration, an option asks whether to use generative orchestration for the agent's responses: yes or no.
In a topic's trigger, generative mode shows the agent chooses, with its description, instead of user says a phrase.
To see what the agent decided, open the test pane and the activity map.
It shows the plan in real time.
One more switch, and it is not yours.
If an administrator turns off generative orchestration in an environment, agents in that environment can only use classic mode.
So if a maker cannot find generative behavior anywhere, even with the agent setting on yes, check the environment.
The environment rule wins over the agent's wish.
Copilot Studio builds agents on more than one harness, the runtime under the agent.
The standard harness uses rule based topics and flows.

The Microsoft Copilot harness, formerly called the GitHub Copilot harness, is built for reasoning heavy, multistep work, with skills, memory, a secure sandbox, and usage based billing in Copilot Credits.
Despite the old name, it is not the GitHub Copilot service.
The Copilot chat harness extends Microsoft Copilot Chat.
An agent cannot move between harnesses.
A Microsoft Copilot harness agent cannot be transferred to the standard harness, and the other way round.
A working standard agent does not need to move just because a new harness exists.
Treat a move as re architecture, a rebuild, and do it only for a clear benefit.
Learn describes the Microsoft Copilot harness as a production ready preview.
Your turn.
Contoso's standard harness agent works well.
A team member wants to switch it to the Microsoft Copilot harness.
What is true?
It cannot be transferred, a move means rebuilding?
It moves by itself when the harness leaves preview?
Or there is a Settings button that converts it?
Decide before I answer.
It cannot be transferred.
A move is re architecture, so only do it for a clear benefit.
On the Microsoft Copilot harness the agent has four tabs.
Build holds identity, knowledge, tools, skills, model and memory.
Preview is for testing.
Evaluate runs test sets that measure quality.
Monitor shows production health, outcomes, reactions, sessions and credit usage.
The life cycle is create, build, test, publish, monitor.
And this harness uses one enhanced orchestration model for all agents, so you cannot configure orchestration like on the standard harness.
Here are the steps.
Open your agent and go to Settings.
In the generative A I section, find orchestration and check that it is set to yes.
Open a custom topic and look at its trigger.
Edit the description: one or two sentences that say what it does and what it does not do.
Check a tool's name and description.
Then type a request with two intentions in the test pane, and open the activity map.
Back to Nexo.
In generative mode, the employee's two wishes became one plan: check the old case, create the new ticket, and answer once.
Remember for the exam: generative chooses by description and name, classic by trigger phrases.
In classic, tools run only from topics.
Overlapping descriptions are unpredictable.
And agents never move between harnesses.
